subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a booking is made.
summary: Eburnean Med Spa's homepage does the fundamentals right for a first-time visitor. The headline — “Enhance Your Natural Beauty at Eburnean Med Spa in Austin, TX” — names the practice and the city in one line, and the opening paragraph lists exactly what is on offer (Botox, microneedling, body contouring and advanced laser treatments) inside the first two sentences. Two clear calls to action sit above the fold on both desktop and mobile: “Book an Appointment” and a “Call 8322584222” button. The phone number, email address and full street address — 12885 Research Blvd Suite #203, Austin, Texas, 78750 — repeat in a header bar that stays visible on every screen.

The clearest opportunity is trust. No practitioner, injector or medical director is named anywhere in the homepage's visible text, and no review or rating appears near either call to action — for Botox and dermal filler specifically, that is usually the detail that turns hesitation into a booking. Two smaller, fixable issues sit close to the top of the page too: the stat row beneath the hero reads “+500 New collections” and “+350 Facial specialist”, wording that reads as leftover template copy rather than a patient-facing claim, and the “Happy customer” and “Year experience” counters both appear in the page's own text as “0 +”.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on desktop and mobile plus the page's own text content. The booking flow was not traced past the button, no treatment page was reviewed, and no Google Business Profile data was checked, so the score is normalised across the categories that were assessed. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Booking-flow depth beyond the button, treatment-page content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. The score is held down mainly by the absence of any named practitioner or visible review — most of the rest of the first screen is close to solid.

scorecard.finding: Headline and location are clear, but the stat row below it reads as mismatched template copy.
No practitioner is named, and no review or rating appears anywhere on the page.
Book and call buttons both sit above the fold on desktop and mobile; the flow past the button was not traced.
One clear action, but nothing sits beside it to reassure a hesitant visitor.
Full-width buttons, readable type, and the header bar repeats phone and email without scrolling.
One address and one phone number, consistent across the header on both breakpoints.

strengthsLead: These are genuine, and the recommendations below build on them rather than replace them.

strengths.title: The headline names the practice and the city in one line.
strengths.body: “Enhance Your Natural Beauty at Eburnean Med Spa in Austin, TX” answers what and where before a visitor has to scroll or hunt. The opening paragraph immediately follows with the treatment list — Botox, microneedling, body contouring, laser — so a first-time visitor is oriented within seconds.

strengths.title: Two clear calls to action, above the fold, on both devices.
strengths.body: “Book an Appointment” and “Call 8322584222” sit side by side in the hero on desktop, and stack full-width on mobile. Neither competes with the other — one is for a visitor ready to book, the other for one who wants to ask a question first.

strengths.title: Contact details repeat in a persistent header bar.
strengths.body: The phone number, email address and full street address appear in a bar above the main navigation on both desktop and mobile, so a visitor never has to scroll to find them. The same number and address appear in the hero and header alike — nothing conflicts.

strengths.title: The “Our Philosophy” copy avoids overclaiming.
strengths.body: “We believe cosmetic treatments should never look overdone” is a modest, credible line for a med spa, and the four bullet points beneath it (personalised plans, subtle results, patient education, long-term skin health) read as genuine values rather than marketing filler.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The hero names Austin, TX directly and carries both calls to action above the fold; the header bar repeats phone, email and full address.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. The header bar leads with phone and email before the logo; both buttons run full width beneath the headline.

findings.heading: No practitioner is named anywhere on the homepage.
findings.evidence: The visible homepage text — hero, About section and Our Philosophy — describes the practice's mission and approach but does not name a physician, nurse injector or medical director at any point.
findings.why: Botox, filler and laser treatments are decisions about a specific person's hands, not only a brand. Without a named, credentialed provider visible early, a hesitant full-fee patient has no answer to the question that usually decides the booking: who is actually doing this to me.
findings.recommended: Name the medical director or lead injector, with a credential and a real photograph, in the About section or near the hero.

findings.heading: No review or rating appears anywhere on the page.
findings.evidence: Neither the homepage text nor either screenshot shows a star rating, review count or testimonial near the booking buttons or anywhere else on the captured content.
findings.why: Proof needs to sit where the doubt is. A visitor deciding whether to book has nothing corroborating “safe and effective” beyond the practice's own description of itself.
findings.recommended: Add a Google rating badge with review count near the primary call to action once the practice has a public rating to show.

findings.heading: The stat row beneath the hero doesn't fit a med spa.
findings.evidence: Directly under the two buttons, the page reads “+500 New collections” and “+350 Facial specialist”. “New collections” is retail-catalogue language, and “Facial specialist” as a count of 350 doesn't read as a coherent patient-facing statistic.
findings.why: This sits in the first screen a visitor sees, right after the two buttons that ask for action. Mismatched or template-sounding labels in that spot read as unfinished, which works against the credibility the rest of the hero is building.
findings.recommended: Replace both labels with statistics that make sense for the practice — years in operation, patients treated, or treatments performed — worded for a patient rather than a shopper.

findings.heading: The “Happy customer” and “Year experience” counters read as zero.
findings.evidence: Further down the homepage text, the labels “Happy customer 0 +” and “Year experience 0 +” appear exactly as written, with “0” where a real figure should be.
findings.why: If this is an animated counter that only fills in on scroll, the underlying page content — what search engines and screen readers read — still says zero happy customers and zero years of experience, which is the opposite of the intended signal.
findings.recommended: Set the real figures as the counters' starting or fallback values so the correct numbers are present in the page content even before any animation runs.

findings.heading: What happens after “Book an Appointment” is clicked wasn't assessed.
findings.evidence: Both screenshots and the homepage text confirm the button exists and is prominent; this review did not trace the booking flow past that button, so whether it completes on-site or hands off to a third-party platform is not established here.
findings.why: The handoff moment — on-brand booking versus a third-party page — is where some patients hesitate or abandon. This is flagged as unassessed rather than scored, so it isn't held against the site without evidence.
findings.recommended: Confirm the booking flow keeps the practice's branding through to confirmation, and that it does not require re-entering information already given.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Standard layout throughout — logo left, nav centre, booking button right on desktop, hamburger menu on mobile. Nothing here surprises a visitor.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: Both the book and call buttons run full width on mobile and are large, well-spaced targets. This is done correctly.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: No review, rating or testimonial was found anywhere on the homepage to place near the decision.
Absent. No practitioner name or credential appears anywhere in the captured content.
Strong. Book or call are the only two actions offered in the hero, and both are unambiguous.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: None observed — no treatment, time or location is pre-suggested to a first-time visitor.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: “We believe cosmetic treatments should never look overdone” is a modest, credible claim — undercut somewhat by the “0 +” counters nearby, which read as unfinished rather than realistic.

roadmap.actions: Fix the “0 +” counters so real figures appear in the page content. Replace “New collections” and “Facial specialist” with statistics that fit a med spa. Confirm the booking button's destination keeps the practice's branding through to confirmation.

Name the medical director or lead injector with a credential and photograph. Add a Google rating badge with review count near the primary call to action. Add one or two short patient testimonials near the hero.

Build out treatment-page depth with candidacy and process information for Botox, microneedling, body contouring and laser. Collect and publish more reviews. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: This review assessed the homepage at 1366×768 and at 390 pixels wide, together with the page's own text content. Treatment-page depth, technical performance, and what happens after the booking button is clicked were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available). No Google Business Profile data was checked; local signals reflect on-page contact information only.
